newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Emergency in northern NZ as cyclone sweeps country.
newsitem.headline: Emergency in northern NZ as cyclone sweeps country.

text.p: A Civil Defence state of emergency was declared in the North Island town of Thames on Saturday as New Zealand reeled under its second tropical storm in as many weeks.
Police in Thames, in the Coromandel region, said around 40 homes had been evacuated by 1 p.m. (2400 GMT on Friday) and with high tide making the situation worse, this number could rise to 90-150.
Residents with their belongings were led through waist-deep water on the streets as waves poured into properties and water seeped through houses, Radio New Zealand reported.

People travelled the streets by canoe as gale-force winds whipped up seas into two to three metre (six to nine feet) swells. Power and sewage pumps were out in some suburbs, with minor sewage contamination occuring.

Meteorological Service forecaster Ian Miller told Reuters that although tropical Cycline Drena was officially downgraded to a deep depression on Friday morning, it was causing widespread damage and the MetService had decided to continue referring to it as a cyclone to prevent complacency.
"Otherwise there's a danger people think its fizzling out... We try to be meteorologically correct but it seems to be causing some confusion. We still haven't seen the last of it," he said.
Meanwhile, clean-up operations were beginning in Auckland, New Zealand's largest city. Drena kept emergency services on the run with power lines down, trees felled and roofs lifted.

Gales battered the region as the cyclone struck late on Friday afternoon, causing widespread damage and flooding. Winds of up to 100 km per hour (62 mph) were recorded on land, and up to 150 km per hour (94 mph) in the Hauraki Gulf.
Auckland police said vehicles were blown across lanes in exposed areas, and some roads had to be closed when they became awash as waves crashed over sea walls.
As the storm died down the coast guard said about eight boats had broken free of moorings and run aground, and it was trying to contact owners to start salvage operations.

MetService forecaster Bob McDavitt said Drena was expected to gather momentum along the Kaikoura Coast on the east of the South Island later on Saturday afternoon, lashing the Kaikoura ranges with up to 50 millimetres (two inches) of rain.
There were no reports of casualties as Drena headed south, less than two weeks after Cyclone Fergus brought torrential rain and heavy flooding to northern areas.
